Hear now the count of twelve lives, stretched across 470 years from year zero to the final breath in year 470. I do not sing of gods who descend, for the record shows three descents of liberated ones, but this song turns on the weight of the wheel itself. It begins with Utnaraj of Narikota, a ruler whose hands knew power until year 34, and ends with Kachiini of Kebhapura, whose death in year 470 broke the chain forever. Between these points lies a road through nine houses: Kriyatirtha, Sudragrama, Narikota, Tugakshetra, Pulikshetra, Rimudesha, Latakota, Gabikshetra, and Kebhapura.

The world turned through the Satya age of the first cycle, then the Treta age of the first cycle, and finally the Dvapara age of the first cycle. In these ages, zero dissolutions of the manifest world marred the sky, yet the soul changed its vessel repeatedly. It was Utnaraj, then Amla of Gabikshetra, a child only from year 36 to 38. It became Kimila of Narikota, a mystic who watched the sun rise for 65 years until 107. It took the shape of Rasumala of Sudragrama, Mishibhat of Gabikshetra, Rishunish of Rimudesha, Gutra of Kebhapura, Pulamini of Rimudesha, Suvaraj of Gabikshetra, Svasarat of Sudragrama, Arshita of Kriyatirtha, and finally Kachiini.

Some lives were brief, like Amla’s or Svasarat’s childhoods, others long and heavy with mastery. You will feel the dust of Narikota and the damp mist of Gabikshetra. You will know the silence of mystics who held their breath against time. The soul carried its burden through each body, learning that freedom is not a gift but a release. In year 470, with the death of Kachiini, it left the wheel forever. Do not ask for more than this twelve-fold journey across 470 years. That is all the record holds.

The soul entered the flesh of Utnaraj in year 0, when the world had just ceased its sleep and stood manifest under the Satya age of the first cycle. He was a man of the house of Narikota, 30 years old before the first stone was set for the first wall, already worn by time that had not yet named itself. The body he inhabited was ruled by craving, a heavy engine that demanded fuel it could never satisfy. He did not know this then, nor did he know that the soul would rise in virtue over the course of this single life, only to find its ruling enemy waiting at the door: anger.

In year 1, when Utnaraj was 31, he bonded with Tradhita. They stayed together for 33 years, a duration marked by the quiet labor of existence rather than grand gestures. It was a long marriage, but it ended in year 34, when Utnaraj’s own heart stopped at 65. The world would call him a ruler, not because he sought the title, but because his weight settled over the house of Narikota like a stone over a grave.

At 36, in year 5, struck by loss, Utnaraj saw the better course and chose the worse. The path was clear, white and straight, but he stepped off it into the mud. He did not stumble; he walked deliberately into the dark. Then came year 13, when he was 44. Crowned by success, he saw the impulse rise within him—a hot, bright thing—and he mastered it. The work of his hands grew steady, the light in his eyes cooled to a manageable gray. He learned that mastery was not a gift but a discipline, a tightening of the muscle against the pull of the wind.

In year 15, at 46, given power, Utnaraj saw the impulse rise and mastered it again. This time he did it in public, before six witnesses who stood silent as statues. The deed was seen as good, and the story of it was told among a few, not out of admiration, but out of the human need to make sense of what it costs to hold oneself together. Yet the soul remembered that over the whole life, there were 31 times the impulse acted unseen, when no eyes watched and no story was told.

In year 16, at 47, struck by loss, Utnaraj saw the impulse rise and mastered it. But in year 27, at 58, crowned by success, he saw the better course and chose the worse. Again, in year 29, at 60, crowned by success, he saw the better course and chose the worse. The pattern was not linear; it was a spiral that sometimes ascended and sometimes descended with equal ease. He lived through years where the right thing was done without struggle, nine such moments of grace amidst the friction of daily survival.

When Utnaraj died in year 34, at 65, the Satya age of the first cycle continued its slow turn. The soul left the body, having risen in virtue, carrying the weight of anger as its final companion. It returned to the unmanifest, to wait for another body, leaving behind only the memory of a man who was among the first, and a life more often swept than steering.

per_chapter.heading: Canto 2: Kimila of Narikota
per_chapter.text:
The third life began not with the clamor of birth but with the quiet settling of dust. It was year 42, in the Satya age of the first cycle, when Kimila came into being within the house of Narikota. She was the daughter of Richita and Amveprala, a child born of lineage that had already tasted the bitter ash of its own history. The soul entered this new vessel ruled by anger, a hot and coiled thing in the belly, distinct from the craving that had driven the previous iteration. There was a gap between these lives, brief and hollow, where the soul had worn the body of Amla of Gabikshetra for 2 years only. Amla was born in year 36 and died as a child, having faced no test, leaving the soul unscarred but hungry for substance.

Kimila grew into the weight of her name. At 19, in year 61, she bonded with Bishanath. Their years together were measured out in seven, until the silence took him in year 68. The loss was a stone in the throat. At 27, in year 69, struck by that deep and resonant loss, Kimila saw the impulse rise—the old anger of the soul, seeking to burn what remained—and she mastered it. She did this in public, before a single witness. The deed was seen as good, and the story of it was told among a few, carried on the wind like chaff.

She then bonded with Utsha. They stayed together 38 years, a long tether against the current of time. During this span, she bore Guka, born in year 87. The world around her continued its slow rotation, indifferent to the internal wars being fought in the quiet rooms of the house of Narikota. At 34, in year 76, struck by loss again, Kimila saw the better course and chose the worse. The path of least resistance is always paved with immediate relief, even if it leads to ruin.

Years accumulated like sediment. In year 94, at 52, Kimila spoke a teaching the world came to call 'Song of Ember'. It was a moment of clarity, a flash of heat that illuminated the dark corners of her experience. What it held has since been lost in the retelling, swallowed by the very uncertainty she had once mastered. At 35, in year 77, given power, Kimila saw the impulse rise and mastered it. At 36, in year 78, lost in uncertainty, she saw the impulse rise and mastered it again. These were small victories, hard-won and easily forgotten.

But the soul was changing. The anger that had ruled at the start of this life began to temper into something more complex, more binding. At 50, in year 92, struck by loss, she saw the better course and chose the worse. At 56, in year 98, struck by loss, she saw the better course and chose the worse. Each choice was a thread pulled tighter.

Kimila died in year 107, at 65, in the Satya age of the first cycle. The world would call her a mystic, mistaking the weight of her attachments for spiritual depth. Over this life the soul rose greatly in virtue, yes, but the ruling enemy at the end was attachment. It clung to the bones of those it loved, to the memories of Bishanath and Utsha, to the ghost of Guka. The soul returned to the unmanifest, to wait for another body, carrying the heavy, warm cargo of a life mostly lived in the shadow of its own desires.

per_chapter.text:
The fourth life began not with a cry, but with the quiet turning of a wheel that had spun through years and ages until its turn came round once more. Rasumala entered the world in year 107, born to Kigamala and Yasan within the house of Sudragrama. She arrived in the Satya age of the first cycle, under a sky that seemed indifferent to the weight she would carry. The soul, still heavy with the residue of its previous existence as Kimila of Narikota, did not arrive empty-handed. It came ruled by attachment, that subtle, clinging force that binds the spirit to the dust of the world.

For decades, Rasumala lived a life mostly at ease, though ease is often a mask for inertia. At 18, in year 125, she bonded with Bichirun. Their union was not a storm, but a long, steady tide. They stayed together for 29 years, a span that measured her youth and her middle age alike. It was a time of shared breath and shared silence, until death claimed Rasumala in year 154 at the age of 47. Before that end, life had given her two children: Chidumala, born in year 146, and Bhakan, born in year 151. These births were anchors, pulling her deeper into the fabric of domesticity.

The soul’s struggle was not with grand enemies, but with small, daily impulses. At 23, in year 130, Rasumala was struck by loss. In that raw moment, she saw the better course clearly, yet she chose the worse. It was a failure of will, a slip into the familiar groove of selfishness. But the soul was learning. At 28, in year 135, lost in uncertainty, she felt the impulse rise like smoke from a hidden fire. This time, she saw it and mastered it. The victory was quiet, internal, but it shifted the weight of her spirit.

The pattern repeated, sometimes breaking, sometimes holding. At 35, in year 142, again lost in uncertainty, she saw the impulse rise and mastered it. By 39, in year 146, struck by loss, she faced the urge to retreat into pain, but she mastered it. Two years later, in year 147, struck by loss once more, she mastered it again. These were not miracles, but the slow hardening of resolve against the softness of desire.

Yet the grip of attachment did not loosen entirely. At 41, in year 148, lost in uncertainty, Rasumala saw the better course and chose the worse. The soul stumbled, dragged down by the very bond that had defined her life with Bichirun. Still, over the whole of her existence, the scales tipped. Four times she saw the impulse and mastered it; three times she saw the light and walked in shadow. Ten times the impulse acted unseen, unnoticed in the blur of habit, but 21 times she did the right thing without struggle.

When she died in year 154, at 47, the world would call her a mystic, mistaking her endurance for enlightenment. But the truth was simpler. Over this life, the soul had risen in virtue. It had fought the ruling enemy, attachment, and though it had not won cleanly, it had advanced. The body grew cold, and the soul returned to the unmanifest, to wait for another body, carrying the scars of its choices into the silence before the next birth.

The wheel turned again. The soul, having shed the heavy skin of Rasumala who had died at 47 in year 154, bound by attachment as before, now sought a new vessel. It came into the house of Gabikshetra, born to Ishdani and Nipuk, and was named Mishibhat in the year 154. The Satya age held its breath, but the soul arrived ruled by attachment once more, carrying the old weight into fresh air.

For years, the days were quiet, filled with the mundane rhythm of breathing and eating, until the mind grew restless. In year 171, when Mishibhat was 17, uncertainty clouded her judgment. She felt the impulse rise within her, a familiar heat seeking to direct her hands and words. Instead of yielding, she watched it. She saw its shape, acknowledged its presence, and mastered it. The moment passed without incident, but the memory of that mastery lingered like a stone in the shoe.

Five years later, in year 173, at age 19, Mishibhat bonded with Suta. They stayed together for 38 years. This bond was not merely social; it was a tether that grounded her in the world even as her spirit looked upward. Yet, in year 174, when she was 20, loss struck again. This time, she was swept along unseeing. The impulse acted before notice could catch it. She moved through the day unaware that her will had been borrowed by desire, a small theft of selfhood committed in the fog of grief.

By year 175, at age 21, loss returned with sharper teeth. Mishibhat saw the impulse rise and mastered it. In the same year, lost in uncertainty, she saw the impulse rise and mastered it again. These were not easy victories; they required a stillness that felt unnatural to the blood. But each time, the soul tightened its grip on the reins.

Decades passed. The body aged, the hair thinned, but the mind remained sharp. In year 200, at age 46, struck by loss, Mishibhat saw the better course and chose the worse. It was a rare stumble, a moment of fatigue where the will gave way to habit. She did not see it as a failure then, only as a weight she could not lift.

In year 208, at age 54, struck by loss once more, she saw the impulse rise and mastered it. The pattern held. She was learning, slowly, how to stand in the storm without being blown away.

In year 304, at age 150, though her body had long since returned to dust in year 211 at age 57 in the Treta age, her teaching remained. The world called it the 'Wheel of Ladder'. She had held that domination does not liberate; restraint, exercised, loosens the wheel’s grip. A soul can leave the wheel forever. This was the fruit of her labor. Over this life, she rose greatly in virtue. Yet, at the end, the ruling enemy was craving, a subtle pull that lingered even as she spoke truth. The soul returned to the unmanifest, to wait for another body, carrying the light it had gathered and the shadow it had not yet shed.

per_chapter.text:
The dust in the house of Gabikshetra tasted of old clay and dried sweat, a flavor Arbhani had known since year 220. It settled in the creases of her palms, in the lines around her eyes, a constant reminder of the earth that held them all. She was born under the weight of the Treta age of the first cycle, a time when the world felt sharp and unyielding, like flint struck against steel. Her father, Chatedat, had hands like roots, gnarled and strong, while her mother, Lapra, moved with a silence that seemed to swallow sound whole. Arbhani grew up in the space between their presence and absence, surrounded by the ghosts of her siblings: Dubha, whose laughter had once filled the courtyard; Utsrishi, who stared at horizons no one else could see; Tevivesh, whose strength was a wall against the wind; and Tapaguni, who held secrets like stones in her pocket.

But it was not their faces that haunted her waking hours. It was the pull, the invisible thread that tugged at her ribs whenever she looked upon another soul. Attachment. The ruling enemy of her birth had whispered to her before she could walk, before she could speak. It was not a shout but a hum, a low vibration in the blood that promised warmth in exchange for bondage. She felt it in the morning light as it crept across the floor, seeking her feet; she felt it in the evening shadows that clung to the pillars like desperate lovers. To resist it required a stillness so profound it felt like death.

The air in the courtyard was thick with the scent of blooming jasmine, sweet and cloying. Arbhani sat on the stone bench, her fingers tracing the cracks in the surface. She remembered the reason she had come to this house, though the words were lost to time, leaving only the residue of things left unresolved. It hung in the air like smoke, indistinct but suffocating. Every interaction was a negotiation with that enemy. When Dubha spoke, Arbhani had to hold her breath until the echo faded. When Lapra touched her shoulder, Arbhani had to steady her own pulse against the sudden flare of affection that threatened to unravel her discipline.

The heat of the day pressed down on the roof tiles, radiating warmth into the stone beneath her. It was a physical weight, grounding her, reminding her of the reality of the body she inhabited. She closed her eyes and listened to the distant sounds of the village: the clatter of pots, the lowing of cattle, the murmur of voices that belonged to others. Each voice was a potential chain, each gaze a hook waiting to catch her soul. She did not fight the feeling with anger or fear. Those were emotions too, and attachments in disguise. Instead, she watched it rise like tide water, observing its height and its retreat, letting it pass through her without taking root.

The sun dipped lower, casting long shadows that stretched across the yard like fingers reaching for her. Arbhani remained still, a statue of flesh and bone amidst the swirling chaos of desire. The Treta age demanded precision, a razor’s edge between existence and dissolution. She breathed in the dust, breathed out the temptation, and waited for the night to bring its own cold clarity. There was no victory here, only endurance. The house stood around her, silent witness to a war fought in silence, where the only casualty was the self, slowly, steadily, being unmade.

per_chapter.text:
The air in the chamber of Gabikshetra was thick, heavy with the scent of aged timber and the metallic tang of fear. Arbhani stood before the low table, her hands trembling not from cold, but from the memory of year 245. At 25, she had been lost in uncertainty, a fog so dense it swallowed reason whole. She had seen the better course clearly, a straight path lined with honor and safety, yet she had chosen the worse. It was not a mistake made in haste, but a deliberate turn toward darkness, a choice that now sat on her shoulders like lead armor. The weight of it pressed against her lungs, making every breath a labor.

Now, at 26, in year 246, the fog had lifted slightly, revealing the precipice she had nearly fallen into again. She saw the impulse rise within her, a hot, coiled thing seeking to unmake her resolve. It felt like hunger, sharp and demanding. But this time, she did not feed it. She mastered it. The suppression was violent, a clenching of the spirit that left her hollowed out but upright. The room seemed to shrink around her, the shadows lengthening as if they too were judging her silence.

By year 247, at 27, the transformation was complete. Success crowned her head, not with gold, but with a terrifying clarity. She had seen the impulse again, that same coiled threat, and she had mastered it once more. The mastery was not gentle; it was a carving out of self, a removal of weakness until only steel remained. In that moment, the drumbeat of her own heart became a rhythm of defiance.

She took up the stylus. Her hand was steady now. She wrote words that tasted of ash and triumph. *Let the elders say what they will,* she inscribed, the ink black against the pale surface. *I was told to kneel in the Treta.* The memory of that order, given when she was young and blind, rose up like a ghost. But she did not bow to it. She continued, her fingers pressing hard into the material. *This drum is my answer.* The rhythm of the words matched the pounding in her chest. *Arbhani will not kneel; the Treta can keep its perfume.*

The word "perfume" hung in the air, cloying and false. It was the scent of submission, of the sweet lies told to keep women quiet. Arbhani set the stylus down. The room felt different now, lighter, yet sharper. She looked at her hands, no longer trembling. They were instruments of will, not vessels for uncertainty. The past remained, heavy and real, but it was hers to carry, not to be crushed by. She turned from the table, walking toward the window where the light of the Treta age filtered in, cold and indifferent. She did not look back.

The dust in the courtyard hung suspended, golden and thick, tasting of dry earth and old stone. Arbhani stood by the low wall, her fingers tracing the rough grit that had settled into her skin over decades. She was 45 now, though the calendar said year 265. The number felt heavy, a weight on her chest that no amount of breathing could dislodge. Jade had been gone for only one year, but the silence he left behind was louder than the market’s clamor, louder than the wind in the date palms.

Jade of Kebhapura. She closed her eyes and tried to summon his face, the curve of his smile, but the memory was fraying at the edges, worn smooth by time like a river stone. The world would call him an opportunist one day, she knew; it was already whispered in the taverns, muttered by rivals who saw only what they wanted to see. But here, in the quiet of her grief, he was just Jade. He had been her bond at 20, in year 240, when the future was a blank page and fear was a cold companion. They had stayed together for 24 years. 24 years of shared breath, shared bed, shared silence. And then, in year 264, he died.

The ache in her ribs tightened, a physical knot that refused to loosen. She looked down at her hands, stained with the ink of ledgers and the dirt of gardens. She had lost him too soon, or perhaps not soon enough. The uncertainty that had driven her to choose the worse course at 25 still lingered, a shadow in the corner of her mind. What if she had chosen differently? What if she had held on tighter?

A figure approached through the haze. Krija. Of the house of Pulikshetra. He moved with a quiet grace that seemed out of place in the harsh sunlight. The world would call him a mystic, Arbhani thought, hearing the echo of future judgments before they were even spoken. But for now, he was just a man walking toward her, his eyes calm, unreadable.

At 45, in year 265, she felt the pull of something new, something dangerous. It was not love, not yet. It was a need to fill the void, a desperate grasp at warmth before the cold could take hold completely. She watched Krija approach, feeling the weight of her own mortality pressing against her skin. She had children—Bachak, Irmumala, Shiki, and little Kutraraj, born in year 265, just as her old life ended. They were scattered in her mind like coins, each one a separate worry, a separate joy.

But here, now, there was only Krija. And the choice before her, silent and inevitable. She did not turn away. She stood her ground, letting the dust settle on her shoulders, feeling the first tremor of a new beginning, terrifying and bright as a struck match in the dark.

The dust of the courtyard tasted of dry earth and old ash. Arbhani stood in the center of the sun-baked stone, her feet rooted against the heat rising through the soles of her sandals. She was 34 years old, or thereabouts; time had become a heavy cloak she wore without complaint. The house of Gabikshetra loomed around her, its walls thick with history and silence. Today, however, the silence felt different. It was not empty. It was full of the roar of success, a noise so loud it drowned out the wind in the date palms.

She had just received the final seal of approval for her latest commission. The elders had nodded. The masters had bowed. Her name was spoken with reverence. Arbhani felt the weight of their admiration settle on her shoulders like a mantle of lead. It was good. It was right. And yet, beneath the warmth of their praise, she felt the cold slickness of desire uncoiling in her gut.

*Take more,* the impulse whispered. *It is yours. You have earned it.*

She saw it clearly now, rising like black smoke from a hidden fire. It was not hunger for food or thirst for water. It was a hunger for more power, more recognition, more of the sweet, intoxicating air that filled her lungs when she walked through the gates as a victor. The impulse demanded she reach out, to grasp the next title, the next honor before it could slip away.

Arbhani closed her eyes. She breathed in the scent of the jasmine vine climbing the trellis above her. It was fragile, sweet, and transient. Just like this moment. She remembered the years before, the long stretches of uncertainty where she had been nothing but a shadow. She remembered the scarcity that had gnawed at her ribs when the harvest failed. And she remembered the first time she had faced this specific demon, at 33, in year 253, when the world was gray and meaningless. She had mastered it then.

But now? Now the temptation was dressed in gold.

She imagined taking the power. Imagine the way it would feel to hold it all in her hands, to bend the will of Gabikshetra to her own. It would be easy. The door was open. No one stood in her way. The impulse surged, a physical ache in her chest, demanding action.

*No,* she thought. Not with words, but with the tightening of her jaw, the straightening of her spine.

She pictured a water-jar, heavy and full, resting on the flat stone beside her well. To pick it up was to carry its weight. To set it down was to let go. She felt the phantom weight of the jar in her hands. The wanting was there, bright and sharp as a shard of glass. But she could feel the path widening behind that release.

She exhaled, long and slow, pushing the smoke out of her lungs. She watched the dust swirl around her feet, then settle. The roar of success faded, replaced by the hum of the wheel turning in the wellhouse nearby. Gabikshetra turned with it. Nothing was lost that was true.

Arbhani opened her eyes. The sun was lower now, casting long shadows across the courtyard. She felt lighter, though she carried nothing but her own body. She walked toward the well, not to drink, but to watch the rope creak as the bucket dipped into the dark water below. The impulse was gone, mastered not by force, but by stillness. She would write it down later, in the quiet of her room, when the ink was black and the paper was white. For now, she simply stood, watching the wheel turn, and let the moment pass.

The wind moves through Gabikshetra, carrying the dust of centuries and the voices of 93 souls who sing 'The Saying of Sateshri'. They do not sing it with malice, but with a heavy certainty that clings like mud to the hem of a robe. Their mouths shape the story of Udjat, for they believe he did ill for the world. The melody is old, worn smooth by repetition, yet each time the song passes from one throat to another, it shifts. It has changed 28 times in the retelling, warping under the weight of memory. Doctrine annexes new limbs to the old trunk. The truth undergoes inversion, turning inside out until light becomes shadow and shadow becomes light. Misattribution takes root like a weed, choking the original stem. The scale of the deed swells and shrinks with the breath of the singer, growing vast in one village and minuscule in the next.

Udjat lived from year 402 to year 490, a mystic of Gabikshetra who walked the same dusty roads now trodden by his singers. He knew no ill will in his heart, only the quiet hum of presence. He was a man of silence, observing the world with eyes that saw too much and spoke too little. Yet the song paints him as a villain, a stain on the tapestry of the realm. The villagers nod along, their faces grim, accepting the distortion as fact because it is easier to blame a ghost than to examine their own hands.

But the record remains, cold and clear, untouched by the song’s warm lies. It says the deed was done by Sateshri of Tugakshetra, a mystic who lived from year 0 to year 45. Sateshri acted not for glory, nor for harm, but for a kindness for a few. The soul that rose in virtue earlier on the wheel now rests in the quiet afterlife, unaware that its small mercy has been twisted into a great crime by those who came later. The singers believe they honor the past by condemning Udjat, yet they erase Sateshri entirely. They trade a complex truth for a simple sin, and in doing so, they lose the only thing that might save them from repeating the error. The song ends, but the misunderstanding begins again.

*We sing our errors until they become truth.*

The soul arrived in this vessel ruled by craving, a hunger that settled deep in the belly and drove the gait. At 31, in year 1, he bonded with Tradhita. They walked together through wet seasons and dry, staying bound for 33 years until his own departure in year 34. The silence left behind was not empty but heavy, a weight that pressed on the chest long after the body cooled.

At 36, in year 5, struck by loss, Utnaraj saw the better course and chose the worse. It was a small thing, perhaps a word unspoken or a step taken toward comfort rather than repair, yet it marked a fracture in the fabric of his character. The body was young, fresh with the potential of a long existence ahead, yet already governed by the gravity of connection and fear of severance. By year 125, at age 18, the hands of Rasumala were still learning their own weight when she bonded with Bichirun. They walked the path together for 29 years, a duration that stretched into habit, binding her days to his presence until her own passing in year 154.

Two sons arrived from this union: Chidumala in year 146 and Bhakan in year 151. Each birth tightened the knot of attachment around the soul's throat. At age 23, in year 130, a sharp blow of loss struck, yet Rasumala saw the better course of release and chose instead the worse path of clinging, seeking to hold the world against its own turning. The light in Gabikshetra did not fall evenly; it pooled on the polished floorboards, leaving corners where shadows held their breath. Arbhani, born in year 220, stood at the threshold of her life within the Treta age of the first cycle. She was 20 years old, a young woman whose existence felt suspended between the memory of Lapra and Chatedat and the weight of four siblings—Dubha, Utsrishi, Tevivesh, and Tapaguni—who moved through the house with their own private gravity. The air inside smelled of dried herbs and the faint, metallic tang of the tools laid out on the shelves.

Her soul arrived here with a history much left unresolved, a gap that seemed to echo in the silence of the rooms. From her first breath, the ruling enemy from birth was attachment, a subtle pressure that tightened around her chest like a noose made of invisible threads. It was not a sudden violence but a slow erosion, a temptation to cling to the comfort of what was known, to the warmth of the hearth, to the faces that had defined her before she could speak.

She watched dust motes dance in a shaft of sunlight, and for a moment, she felt the pull to reach out and grasp one of them, to hold onto it until it stopped moving. That was the nature of attachment: the desire to freeze time, to stop the flow of days so that no change could alter the shape of the world as she knew it. Yet, the wind shifted outside, rattling the shutters, and the dust resumed its drift.

Outside the house, the landscape of the Treta age stretched out in hues of ochre and deep green. The people moved with a familiarity born of generations, yet every path offered a choice. Arbhani knew that if she chose to stay exactly as she was, to refuse the shift of seasons, she would eventually be trapped by the very thing she sought to avoid. The weight of the choice rested on her tongue before it was spoken, heavy and unfamiliar.

Dubha called out from the inner room, asking for water. Tevivesh adjusted his sash near the doorway. No one spoke of the soul's ruling enemy or the unresolved past that defined their lineage; such things were felt, not declared. To speak them aloud would be to declare a war that had been fought silently within the marrow of their bones. The temptation was quiet, however: the comfort of remaining silent about the struggle, of pretending the threads were loose enough to be untied without effort.

Arbhani turned from the window, the cool air on her skin grounding her. She walked to the center of the room, where the floorboards groaned under her feet—a sound as old as the house itself. The light faded slightly as the sun dipped lower, casting long shadows that seemed to stretch toward the past and the future equally. There was no grand revelation, no sudden shift in destiny, only the simple fact of being here, now, with a heart that remembered what it had not yet lived.

The choice remained unmade for another hour, then another, until the call of duty or necessity would pull her forward again. The attachment waited, patient and hungry, but so did the possibility of letting go. In the Treta age of the first cycle, year 220 marked her entry, but the story of how she navigated the waters of her own soul was still unwritten, unfolding in the space between breaths.

The dust of Gabikshetra settled on her shoulders, a grey weight that felt heavier than the wool of her shawl. It was year 247, and she stood at 27, the number etched in the memory of her house like a scar. The air smelled of dry reeds and the lingering heat of midday, but beneath it lay the cold scent of uncertainty she had known since turning 15. She remembered the better course clearly, the path that wound straight toward safety and silence, yet her feet had marched into the darker thicket at 25, in year 245. That choice had tasted like ash, a bitter realization that seeing the light did not grant the power to walk it.

Now, the impulse rose again, physical and demanding, pressing against her ribs like a fist seeking entry. It was not a whisper but a roar, the same hunger that had driven her mother's kin through ages past. She could feel the tension in her jaw, the way her breath hitched before she let it out. To yield would be easy; to kneel would be to accept the old order without question, to let the elders dictate the shape of her life until she dissolved into their shadow. But the drum beat inside her chest, a frantic rhythm that mocked the slow turning of the seasons.

She looked toward the gathering of men who spoke with authority, their voices low and resonant as they discussed the perfumes of the Treta age. They expected submission, a bowing of the head that acknowledged the fragility of things. They wanted her to accept that she was small, that the world was vast and indifferent, and that kneeling was the only rational response to such grandeur. The temptation to kneel was not born of fear alone, but of comfort; the earth offered a soft place to rest, and silence offered a peace that required no fighting.

Yet, Arbhani tightened her grip on her staff. She had composed the words for them yesterday, a hymn that burned in her throat like fire, ready to be spoken only if she dared. The thought of speaking it filled her with a terrifying clarity. If she were to speak, the silence would shatter, and the perfumed air of the Treta would turn to smoke. She had seen the impulse rise at 26, in year 246, and mastered it then, but mastery was not surrender; it was the forging of steel against the anvil of doubt.

The choice remained suspended in the space between her breaths, a moment where time held its breath. The elders could say what they would; their words had weight, yes, but they carried no magic that could bind her spirit to the ground. She felt the better course receding, a distant shoreline she could no longer reach without changing her nature. To choose the worse path now was not to fail, but to assert a reality where her own will was the law. The drum beat louder, syncing with her heart until there was no distinction between the two. She would not kneel. The Treta could keep its perfume, for she belonged to the age of fire now.

The dust in the room of Gabikshetra tasted of old earth and dried lavender, settling thickly on the wooden lintel. Arbhani stood at 25, her hands resting against the grain where it had settled over decades of turning seasons. The year was 245, and uncertainty hung in the air like a wet woolen cloak, heavy and suffocating. She could feel the better course pulling at her shoulder, invisible but undeniable, offering the path of stability. Yet, beneath that pull, she felt the magnetic drag of the worse choice, a dark current drawing her toward the precipice. The temptation did not shout; it simply existed as a cool shadow against her skin, promising a freedom that had no name yet demanded everything.

She remembered the house of Kebhapura, where Jade stood waiting. He was 20 years old when they bonded in 240, his eyes bright with a sharp calculation that the world would later label an opportunist. For four years since their union in 240, he had been her anchor, though she knew that anchor was made of shifting sand. The bond lasted 24 years total, spanning from 240 until his death in 264. In those years, the house had grown with children: Bachak arrived in 253, followed by Irmumala in 258, and Shiki in 263. Each birth was a weight added to her chest, a physical reminder of time passing. Now, standing at the edge of 245, she held the memory of Jade's hand while feeling the ghost of the future pressing against her back.

The light filtered through the high window, illuminating motes that danced like dust devils in a jar. She could hear the distant call to prayer or the clatter of pots in the courtyard, sounds of a life lived and accepted. But here, in this suspended moment, the calculus was brutal. To choose Jade was to accept the known decay, to walk into the darkening hall where his end awaited in 264. To turn away was to embrace the unknown, to risk the loss of the 24 years already woven into her bones.

She did not speak to him; he was not there to hear the hesitation that raked across her spine. The choice sat between her heartbeats, a stone balanced on a knife edge. She thought of the faceless future beyond 245, where paths would diverge like river branches. If she chose stability, she might live through many more winters with Jade. If she chose otherwise, she might lose years to grief or gain them to solitude. The weight of that decision felt less than a full pound but more than a grain of sand; it was the precise tension in a bowstring pulled back to its limit.

Outside, the sun began its descent, casting long shadows that stretched across the threshold she stood upon. The air grew cooler, carrying the scent of rain from a sky far away. She closed her eyes for a heartbeat, feeling the better course whisper against one ear and the worse choice hum against the other. There was no god in this room to weigh their scales, only the raw physics of consequence. She turned slightly, the fabric of her tunic shifting with the movement, marking the end of indecision. The year 245 marked not just a time on a calendar but a fracture in her life where one history ended and another began, unasked for and unwritten until she stepped forward.

The air inside the house of Gabikshetra carried the dust of three decades, settling on the floorboards where Arbhani stood at 62. Outside, the wind tugged at the eaves, but the interior felt heavy with a specific kind of stillness, the quiet that follows many choices made. At this age, the impulse rises less as a storm and more as a current beneath the skin, something she has known since year 253, when at 33 she saw it surge through her chest and mastered it without flinch. Now, standing in the dim light of year 297, the sensation was familiar yet distant, a ghost of her own making.

She turned to the small fire pit where Krija sat, their bond forged 32 years prior at 45. The woman looked older than the calendar dictated, though the record does not speak of this age specifically, only that Arbhani lived until year 297. The warmth of the flames did little to chase away the chill of scarcity that had visited them before in year 266, when at 46 Arbhani faced hunger and mastered the rising demand for more. That memory tasted like ash and iron, sharp enough to etch itself into the mind. Krija stirred the coals with a rod of blackened wood, her movements economical, practiced.

"Gabikshetra turns," Arbhani said softly, watching the embers shift. It was an old phrase, one she had sung at 38 in year 258, born from a moment years prior when at 34, crowned by success, she saw the impulse and mastered it. The song remained etched in her memory: *Arbhani set down the wanting like a water-jar, / and the path grew quiet / the wheel turns; Gabikshetra turns with it; nothing is lost that was true.*

She recalled year 259, the time at 39 when facing scarcity she saw the better course and chose the worse. It had been a choice of flesh and blood, not abstract philosophy. The temptation then felt like a hand gripping the wrist, urging forward toward safety even if it meant turning away from what was right. She remembered the weight of that decision pressing on her shoulders, the way the future narrowed until only one path remained visible. That regret had been a stone in the shoe, grinding with every step taken since.

Now, at 62, the temptation felt different. It was not a hand but a voice, whispering that the wheel would stop spinning soon enough if she did not push harder. She saw the impulse rise, as it had in year 257 when given power at 37, and again in year 269 when given power at 49. Each time, she had met it with a stillness that felt like holding one's breath underwater. The mastery cost her sleep, her ease, sometimes pieces of herself that never returned. But the alternative was worse.

Krija looked up, eyes reflecting the dying light. "The wheel turns," she said simply.

"It does not stop," Arbhani replied, watching the shadows lengthen across the room. "Nothing is lost that was true."

She thought of year 240, when at 20 she bonded with Jade, and the 24 years they shared until her death in year 264. Those memories were not pain, but anchors. They held her against the pull of new desires. The house felt larger now, filled with the echoes of lives lived fully within its walls. She did not need to explain why she chose the harder path again; the weight of it was sufficient instruction. The fire crackled, sending a spark upward that caught on the smoke hole and vanished into the night. The room settled around them, heavy and real, containing the sum of years 220 to 297 in the silence between breaths.

A woman of the house of Gabikshetra came into the world in year 154, her name Mishibhat, born to Ishdani and Nipuk under the light of the Satya age. This birth was not arbitrary; the turn on the wheel had come round once more, and it landed the soul in a body ruled by attachment, distinct from the quiet mastery of Rasumala's previous existence. The years flowed like water over her hands, carrying her through ages measured in centuries. At 17, in year 171, uncertainty gripped her chest like a sudden cold wind, yet the impulse rose there to be mastered before it could shape the world. But at 20, in year 174, loss struck without warning; swept along unseeing, the impulse acted before she could notice its arrival, dragging her forward as if pulled by an invisible thread.

The path grew harder. At 21, in year 175, the pattern repeated with terrifying consistency. First, loss struck, and the impulse rose to be mastered, a small victory over the tide. Moments later, lost in the same uncertainty, she saw the impulse rise again and mastered it, as if the lesson demanded doubling the effort. It was not until year 200 that a different choice took hold; at 46, struck by loss once more, she saw the better course standing clear before her eyes, yet chose the worse, letting the wheel tighten its grip. Only later, at 54 in year 208, did she master the impulse again when it rose from the depths of another blow.

For 38 years, she had bonded with Suta, their lives intertwined until her own death came in year 211 at the age of 57. In that final twilight of the Treta age, she spoke a teaching that would echo through generations, called by the world the Wheel of Ladder. She held that domination did not liberate, but restraint, when exercised with true intent, loosens the wheel's grip; she taught that a soul can leave the wheel forever. Over this life, the soul rose greatly in virtue, shedding the heavy armor of attachment that had bound her predecessors. The ruling enemy at the end was craving, burned away by the accumulated light of her choices. She died in year 211, and though the years were short compared to those who had walked before, the work was done. The soul returned to the unmanifest, waiting quietly for another body.

The air in the room held the damp weight of a Treta morning, heavy with the kind of silence that presses against the eardrum like deep water. Arbhani sat by the hearth, her hands resting on knees that trembled not from cold but from the internal friction of something she could not yet name. She was year 220 old in spirit now, though her body moved with the fluid grace of youth, born into the house of Gabikshetra under a sky that seemed to swallow the light whole. Her father Chatedat stood near the threshold, his shadow stretching long across the worn floorboards, while her mother Lapra moved among the vessels and woven mats, her presence a quiet current in the stillness.

The memory of birth did not arrive as an event but as a texture, a rough fabric woven into the very marrow of her existence. She felt the pull of the house's old stories, the unspoken laws that guided the feet of others without naming them. Her siblings—Dubha, Utsrishi, Tevivesh, Tapaguni—existed in the background, their laughter and arguments dissolving into the mist of the season. They were part of the tapestry, but she felt the thread of her own soul tangled tightly with the knot of attachment. It was not a physical chain but a feeling of being drawn toward things that had weight and permanence, a desperate hope that mirrored the dust motes dancing in the shafts of light.

The enemy from birth sat quietly on her chair, unseen yet demanding space. It whispered that holding onto anything would bring safety, that the world was fragile enough to be grasped. She could taste the temptation in the air, sweet and cloying like the unripened fruit hanging outside. To let go felt like breathing into a sealed chest; to hold felt like finding solid ground. The choice before her was not spoken aloud but lived in the tightness of her chest and the heat rising from her palms.

Outside, the world of year 220 spun its slow, indifferent cycle. The Treta age continued, indifferent to her internal storm. There were no gods shouting commands in this house, no numbers written in blood on the walls. Only the weight of what remained unsaid hung between them, a space where the soul waited to see if it could ever truly leave the grip of what it loved. Lapra turned a page of an old book, the paper crinkling softly, while Chatedat watched the rain begin to streak the windowpane. In that moment, Arbhani felt the full extent of her own unraveling, the terrifying beauty of being caught between the desire to hold and the knowledge that letting go was the only way to feel whole.

The air in the chamber of Gabikshetra felt heavy with the residue of dust motes dancing in a single shaft of afternoon light, thinning the silence until it pressed against the eardrums. Arbhani stood at the threshold of her twenties, though the world outside these walls had already claimed more than its share of her time. Year 245 loomed like a horizon she could not yet see clearly, a place where uncertainty did not whisper but hammered, demanding a choice between what looked better and what felt right. She had seen the better course before her eyes softened into it, knowing which path would lead to honor, yet she chose the worse. The decision hung in the room like an unlit incense coil, waiting for smoke, heavy with a cost she could not yet weigh but which settled deep within her bones.

By year 246, at 26, the impulse had risen again, rising from somewhere inside the house of Gabikshetra, stirring through the floorboards and the breath held in shared lungs. It was not merely a thought; it was a pressure against the ribs, a desire to speak when silence was expected. She saw it rise again, the same tide returning with new force, and she mastered it. The act of mastery felt less like victory and more like walking through water that had turned cold, each step requiring breath and will before the surface broke.

In year 247, at 27, the room changed. Success crowned her, a weight that shifted from burden to proof. She looked at the drum resting on the altar of old customs, its skin taut with the expectation of submission. The elders would have their say, they would demand the kneeling in the Treta age, but she had already answered before they could speak. A hymn of fury took shape, born from that moment where the impulse was finally silenced and replaced by something sharper. The words formed not on paper or stone, but in the space between heart and throat: "let the elders say what they will: / I was told to kneel in the Treta; / this drum is my answer / Arbhani will not kneel; the Treta can keep its perfume." The scent of that perfume remained, lingering in the air long after the last syllable had died, marking the house with a defiance that did not ask for forgiveness but demanded to be remembered.

The air in the chamber held the weight of 24 years that had already slipped through Arbhani's fingers like sand, yet the room itself seemed older than that, its dust motes dancing in a light that felt too sharp for this hour. At 20, in year 240, she had bonded with Jade, and for so long the warmth of his presence had been the only thing that made the house of Kebhapura's reputation feel like a story told by strangers rather than a truth lived inside her own bones. They were together when the seasons turned most violently, and even now, in her twenties, the memory of that choice did not sit as a settled stone but as a question pressed against her chest, demanding an answer that had already been spoken. The world would one day call him an opportunist, they would say, tracing the name back to a moment where she saw the better course and chose the worse, yet here in the silence, Arbhani felt only the hollow ache of what was left behind when Jade died in year 264.

It had been 24 years since the bond dissolved, and now she stood before Krija, who came from the house of Pulikshetra and whose name would eventually carry a weight the world reserved for mystics, though that title felt foreign to her own life. At 45, in year 265, they had bonded, and for years the air between them tasted different, less like dust and more like a quiet promise held in shared breath. They stayed together 32 years until the end came, but as Arbhani looked at him now, she felt the ghost of those intervening decades pressing against her mind. The children were gone, grown into adults with their own paths, leaving behind only the echoes of Bachak's laughter from year 253, Irmumala's silence from year 258, Shiki's steps from year 263, and Kutraraj from year 265.

The choice before her was not one of grand gestures but of a simple alignment, the kind that felt like stepping into a current that would pull them toward a new shore. To bond again was to accept the uncertainty again, to feel the familiar tremor in her hands that came with knowing exactly how long she had left. Yet as the years counted down from 297, she found herself drawn not by fear but by the profound relief of finally answering the question she could never stop asking. The light in the room seemed to shift, revealing a texture to the walls she had not noticed before, and with it came a clarity that stripped away the need for judgment or explanation. She was simply Arbhani of Gabikshetra, living through the final chapters of a story written long before she understood the ink.

The dust in the room held the weight of unspoken years, settling deep into the creases of Arbhani's hands, which had carried power from age 32 to age 62. It was a quiet house, smelling of dried oil and old stone, where the silence pressed against her eardrums like water against a submerged hull. At 46, in year 266, scarcity had found them again, not as a guest but as a tenant demanding space. The air was thin, tasting of ash that had once been wind. She stood before the hearth, feeling the raw tremor of the impulse rise within her chest, a desperate hunger to seize more than her hands could hold. Yet she watched it swell, saw the shape it took, and chose instead to let it burn without striking flint.

The cost was not a shout but a shift in the light, a sudden dimming that made the walls feel closer than they had been before. She remembered year 259, when facing scarcity had forced her to see the better course only by choosing the worse, trading hope for survival. Now, at 49, given power that felt heavier than lead, she saw the impulse rise once more, a familiar phantom begging for command. She mastered it, not by defeating it with force but by accepting its presence as part of the room's texture, letting it hum against her skin until it found no purchase.

Time moved in circles within this house, yet Arbhani felt herself growing older with every breath. From age 30 to age 62, the years had stacked up like stones at the riverbank, each layer denser than the last. She composed a song of peace that night, born from the memory of when, at 34, crowned by success, she had finally seen the impulse and mastered it for good. The words rose from her tongue, not as commands but as observations of how things held together: "Arbhani set down the wanting like a water-jar, / and the path grew quiet / the wheel turns; Gabikshetra turns with it; nothing is lost that was true."

In year 258, at 38, those words had formed, capturing a moment when certainty had been enough to drown out the rising noise. The house seemed to exhale now, the dust settling into perfect stillness. There were no other paths here, only the steady rotation of Gabikshetra, turning with it, carrying the weight of years that had been mastered not by erasure but by integration. The wheel turned, and so did she, older than the record of her birth would ever show, yet never alone in the quiet.

The soul required twelve lives to be freed from the wheel. In the first life, a woman named Rasumala of Sudragrama walked through years marked by attachment. At 23, struck by loss, she saw the better path but chose the worse, letting craving rule her. She rose in virtue yet remained bound. The next life belonged to Mishibhat of Gabikshetra, another woman and mystic, spanning years 154 through 211. Here the soul rose greatly in virtue but was still ruled by craving. At 46, struck again by loss, she saw the better and chose the worse. Her path mirrored the first; the pattern held tight. Then came Rishunish of Rimudesha, a mystic whose years ran 211 to 235. The soul ended much as it began, ruled by craving. At 18, however, given power, she did the right thing without effort. Yet even this moment of ease could not sever the bond fully. Pulamini of Rimudesha followed, a woman and mystic living years 241 to 321. Her soul rose in virtue again, yet it was ruled by craving. At 18, given power, she too did the right thing without effort. The shadow of loss remained long enough to tempt. Suvaraj of Gabikshetra took the next turn, a man and mystic from years 321 to 364. His soul ended much as it began, ruled by craving. At 30, given power, he did the right thing without effort. Each life offered a glimpse of mastery, but attachment kept the cycle turning.

Arshita of Kriyatirtha came next, a woman and mystic in years 366 to 408. Her soul ended much as it began, ruled by craving. At 17, given power, she did the right thing without effort. The light shone on her hands, yet the wheel spun onward. Kachiini of Kebhapura followed, a woman and mystic living years 408 to 470. Her soul ended much as it began, ruled by craving. At 43, given power, she did the right thing without effort. With the death of Kachiini in year 470, the soul left the wheel forever. The final breath released what was held for so long.

The lesson is that even when you do the right thing without effort, attachment holds the key.

per_chapter.heading: The Fall
per_chapter.text:
The wheel turns again, but with a heavier tread now that the lower lives have taken hold. The soul remains bound, dragged down into the dark grooves of desire and wrath, far from the light where virtue once lived in its earlier forms. It remembers Krishushri of Kebhapura, a woman who walked the earth as a ruler between years 199 and 271, ruling not with love but with a fire that burned cold within her breast. She saw the impulse to destroy others rise up like smoke, a tempting draft promising power she did not need. At 48, she felt the pull of that dark hunger, yet her hands were strong enough to master it, to hold back the flame before it could consume her own breath. Her virtue rose then, a thin silver thread against the storm.

But the wind has changed direction now. The soul has descended into the house of envy, where it cannot sleep until it compares itself with every shadow that passes. First came Dhike of Gabikshetra, another woman who became ruler between years 271 and 328. She stood young at 17 when power was poured into her hands by the indifferent world. The impulse to tear down neighbors surged through her veins, a sudden thirst for blood she could not name. Yet she saw it clearly in the mirror of her own reflection, and with a gasp she mastered it, refusing to let the envy feed the beast within her. Still, the decline had already begun, a slow rot eating at the foundations of what little remained good.

Then came Dhayakrish of Kebhapura, a man who ruled between years 328 and 398. He was 26 when he seized the throne, his eyes fixed on the empty space where others had been. The impulse to make others small rose in him like a fever. He saw it clearly, felt the coldness of that victory, and mastered it again, forced by some unseen hand to check the rising tide of his own contempt. Yet the soul declined further with each passing year, slipping into the deep waters of anger.

Now the path leads to Hamemala of Rimudesha, a woman who walked as an opportunist between years 398 and 495. She fell far, leaving virtue behind her like dry leaves in the wind. Her heart was ruled by anger, a fierce beast that did not care for order or balance, only for the thrill of destruction. At 61, she was struck by loss, a blow that should have been a lesson but became a weapon. She saw the better path before her eyes, yet she chose the worse, turning her face from the light into the darkening void where she waited to end her own story. When the record closes, the soul waits in the unmanifest, ruled by anger, waiting for the next wheel of time to drag it further down, further away from the peace it once knew.

*To love is harder than to hate.*

The air hangs still over Tugakshetra, where the earth remembers the weight of hands that sought only to lift a single star. A song called The Saying of Sateshri moves through the village halls, carried by 93 voices who know the words well and the silence better. It speaks of Udjat of Gabikshetra, a mystic named in the years 402 to 490, claiming he did ill for the world. But the record holds the true shape of the deed, done by Sateshri of Tugakshetra, who walked between years zero and 45 as a figure of quiet mystery. To call Udjat guilty is a kindness granted to only a few, a mercy that wraps error in the wool of truth while the rest remain untouched by it.

The song has turned its face 28 times in the telling, shifting through doctrines, inverting names, misattributing deeds until the scale tips on every new verse. The soul of Sateshri did not seek glory; she sought to bind a fracture within the world's heart, and Udjat was the vessel that broke. When the impulse rose to master it, the light fell not as sun but as a sharp edge cutting through the mist of memory. To rule by envy is to see only what is stolen, yet here the act was a giving back, a restoration so complete it became the ruin of those who feared the gift. The hands that built were few, yet their work spread like ink in water, darkening the waters where no other soul could swim without fear.

The record remembers the cost: the price paid in names and years, the precise measure of time when magic was measured not by breath but by consequence. Sateshri of Tugakshetra stood at the edge of the known world, while Udjat of Gabikshetra remained a shadow cast by her own light. The lesson is not in the song's many turns but in the single truth that rises from the silence between them.

*Truth wears the face of sin to save those who cannot see.*

Listen to the concrete truth of that release, the quiet close of a long road.

He was born in the house of Narikota, at the very beginning of year 0, when the Satya age turned its first leaf. The world was young then, and so was he. But within the quiet chambers of his heart, a different seed had taken root before his first breath: craving. It was not yet a fire, but a shadow, a cold hunger that would outlast his bones.

For 33 years, Utnaraj moved through the days with a strange companionship. He bound himself to Tradhita in year 1, when he was three years old. They walked together through the long arc of his youth and manhood. Their bond did not break until his death in year 34, a span of 33 years that felt both fleeting and eternal. In those years, he learned the weight of another’s hand in his own. He learned that loyalty was a discipline as sharp as any blade.

But the shadow within him stirred. At age 36, in year 5, the test came. It was a moment where the right path lay clear and bright, yet he turned away. He chose worse. The temptation was not loud; it was a whisper that sounded like truth. He gave into it, and the loss was immediate, though invisible to others.

Years passed. At age 44, in year 13, another test arrived. This time, he resisted. He mastered the impulse. It was a small victory, a stone placed in a river of mud. He stood firm when the current pulled hard.

By age 46, in year 15, power came to him. It was not given; it was taken, or perhaps found waiting. He held it for six weeks. During that short span, he did good, but he told few of his deeds. The work of his hands spoke louder than his voice. He moved through the city like a ghost, present but unseen, shaping outcomes without claiming them.

In year 16, at age 47, loss struck again. Yet he mastered it. He absorbed the blow without breaking. There was no drama in his grief, only a quiet endurance that became part of his structure.

But the craving returned with the seasons. At age 58, in year 27, success tempted him. He saw the path of ease, the path that would satisfy the hunger. He chose worse. The temptation was sweet, like ripe fruit hanging just out of reach but within grasp if one dared to climb. He climbed, and he fell.

At age 60, in year 29, success came again. It was easier this time, or perhaps he was more tired. He chose worse once more. The pattern held: three times he mastered the test, three times he chose the downward slope, and 31 times he was swept by the current, acting without steering, living in the wake of forces larger than his will.

When his heart stopped in year 34, at age 65, Utnaraj did not fade into nothingness immediately. The virtue he had accumulated, rose like mist from the earth, lifted him for a moment. He was a ruler in spirit, even if his power had been fleeting. His enemy was anger, or the craving that fed it. But the record ends not with judgment, but with waiting. He awaited rebirth. The unmanifest world opened its doors, and he stepped through, carrying the weight of Narikota, the memory of Tradhita, and the dust of the Satya age on his clothes. He did not know he would return. He only knew the cycle had not ended.

Kimila was born in year 42, within the Satya age of the first cycle. He entered the world as a child of Narikota, son to Richita and Amveprala. The soul had come into this body ruled by craving, a familiar burden from its previous existence as Utnaraj. That earlier life, ending in anger at age 65 in year 34, felt distant now, like dust settling on an old shelf. Here was Kimila, young and eager, with much left unresolved in his spirit.

In year 61, Kimila was 19 years old. He formed a bond with Bishanath. It was a time of clarity, or so it seemed. They walked together through the sun-drenched streets of Narikota, speaking of duty and the earth. This alliance lasted for seven years, until the death of Bishanath in year 68. The loss was sharp, a stone dropped into still water, rippling outward until it touched the shores of Kimila’s own mortality.

By year 69, Kimila was 27. He entered a deeper bond with Utsha. This union would span 38 years, lasting until his own death in year 107. The days passed with a heavy, sweet rhythm. They worked the land, raised their son Guka, who arrived in year 87, and navigated the intricate politics of their house. But the soul within Kimila was not yet free.

In year 69, facing a loss at age 27, Kimila mastered himself. He kept the public grief to one week’s time and told only a few people his true sorrow. It was a disciplined act, a wall built against the flood of emotion. But discipline is not wisdom. In year 76, when he was 34, he faced another loss and chose worse paths. The walls he had built crumbled under the weight of his own impulses. He sought comfort in things that offered no sustenance, acting as if the earth itself were a distraction from the pain.

Year 77 brought power to Kimila at age 35. He mastered this new authority, shaping it with care, ensuring it served rather than corrupted. Yet, in year 78, at age 36, uncertainty arose. He mastered that too, standing firm while others wavered. Mastery became a habit, a tool for smoothing the rough edges of existence.

But mastery is not liberation. In year 92, at age 50, he faced loss and chose worse again. The pattern repeated, a loop of error and correction that never broke the chain. Year 98 brought another loss at age 56, and once more, he chose worse. Each time, he recovered, each time he stumbled, but the core of him remained bound to craving.

In year 94, Kimila, aged 52, taught a teaching called the Song of Ember. It held the lesson that all is lost, a truth he knew intellectually but could not feel in his bones. He preached it while living a life mostly at ease, comfortable in his skin, respected by his peers, yet internally tethered to desires that would not quiet.

In year 107, Kimila died at age 65. The role of mystic had been assumed, the virtue rose greatly in those who remembered him. But his enemy was attachment, and it held fast. He did not break free. He unmanifested, awaiting rebirth, the cycle continuing with the same heavy, concrete grace as before.

The enemy remained attachment, the old wound that never quite healed, waiting for the first opportunity to bleed.

It was not a meeting of thunder or fate’s grand design, but a slow, inevitable drawing together. They did not speak of eternity; they spoke of the day’s work, the price of grain, the way the light hit the river stones. For 29 years, until death took Rasumala in year 154, that bond held. It was a quiet tether, pulling him through the mundane arithmetic of survival and affection.

It was not a malicious choice, merely a tired one, a surrender to the path of least resistance when the spirit was too heavy to lift itself. The lesson lay buried in the dirt, unacknowledged for years.

Then came year 135, age 28. Uncertainty wrapped around him like a cold sheet. He did not panic. He did not rage. He mastered it, standing firm while the world blurred at the edges, finding clarity in the stillness of his own will. It was a small victory, barely noticed by anyone but himself.

In year 142, at age 35, uncertainty returned with greater ferocity. Once more, he mastered it. The skill was becoming muscle memory, the resistance to chaos growing stronger with each iteration. He moved through the years with a steady hand, until year 146 brought another test. Loss struck again, and this time, he mastered it. The grief did not vanish, but it no longer controlled him.

But in year 148, at age 41, uncertainty crept back in. This time, he chose worse. The will faltered, the spirit tired, and he slipped into the old patterns. The role of mystic was fulfilled, the virtue of rose blooming quietly in the heart. Attachment had been faced, again and again, mastered three times, resisted once, succumbed twice. The ledger balanced not in numbers, but in the quiet dignity of a life lived mostly at ease. The soul withdrew from the body, unmanifest, awaiting the next turn of the wheel.

The air of Gabikshetra was thick with the scent of turning seasons, a world caught in the slow, grinding gears of time. This body was not an accident but a necessity; its turn on the wheel had come round, demanding another circuit of struggle and sensation. Born to Ishdani and Nipuk within the house of Gabikshetra, Mishibhat carried the weight of previous attachments like stones in a pocket, heavy and unyielding. The enemy was still attachment, that ancient, clinging vine that sought to root itself in the heart before the feet could even walk.

In year 173, when Mishibhat was just 19, a bond formed with Suta. It was not a firestorm, but a steady kindling. For 38 years, until death took him, they walked side by side. The days were measured in shared silences and the quiet work of living. Yet, the soul’s nature was volatile, prone to sudden shifts in the weather of the spirit.

At 17, in year 171, uncertainty rose like fog from the riverbed. It threatened to blind Mishibhat, to make every step a guess. But the soul mastered it. The mind cleared. The path remained visible, though faint. Two years later, at 20, loss struck in year 174. It was not a grand tragedy, but a sharp pinch, a sudden absence that left a cold space in the chest. The soul swept past it, acting as if nothing had changed, moving with the inertia of habit until the shock wore off.

By 21, in year 175, loss returned, and with it, uncertainty. The twin shadows lengthened. But again, the soul mastered them. There was no dramatic battle, only a quiet refusal to yield ground. The grip held firm. For decades, the life flowed easily. There were years of effortless grace, where the right choice required no struggle at all, like breathing in clean air. The soul navigated the middle courses with ease, avoiding the sharp edges of extreme emotion.

But the wheel does not stop turning because one has learned to balance. At 46, in year 200, loss came again. This time, the soul chose worse. It was a small failure, a momentary lapse into anger or despair, a decision that tightened the knot rather than loosening it. It was a slip on the wet stone, insignificant in itself but damning in its implication. The soul stumbled, and for a brief moment, the grip of the wheel tightened around the ankle.

Yet, by 54, in year 208, loss appeared once more. This time, the soul mastered it. The previous failure had not undone the work; it had merely provided texture. The lesson was absorbed, not repeated. The mastery was deeper now, rooted in experience rather than instinct.

In year 304, when Mishibhat was 150, the teaching emerged: the Wheel of Ladder. It held a simple truth that defied the world’s noise. It was not so that domination liberates; domination only binds. Restraint, exercised consistently, loosens the wheel’s grip. A soul can leave the wheel forever, but only by letting go of the need to hold on.

When death came in year 211, at age 57, Mishibhat’s virtue had risen greatly. The enemy was craving, the final tug that pulls the soul back into the cycle. But this time, the pull was weak. The outcome was unmanifest. The soul awaited rebirth, not with fear, but with the quiet expectation of a traveler who knows the road well, carrying only the memory of the ladder and the lightness of released hands.

The air in Gabikshetra hung heavy, thick with the dust of a some years and the weight of an ending cycle. It was year 220, a time when the world still breathed with the chaotic vitality of the Treta age. Arbhani sat on the floor, her spine rigid, the hardness of the packed earth pressing against her knees through thin cloth. She was born into this house, into this moment, under the gaze of Lapra and Chatedat, whose names were etched into the very stones of their home like scars.

Around her, the silence was not empty; it was crowded with the ghosts of what had not been done. There was so much left unresolved, a tangled knot in the chest that refused to loosen. It felt like a stone swallowed whole, cold and smooth, resting at the bottom of her stomach. She could taste the metallic tang of unfinished business on her tongue.

Dubha was moving somewhere down the corridor, her footsteps a soft rhythm against the silence. Utsrishi’s laughter, bright and sharp, drifted from the courtyard, followed by the low murmur of Tevivesh. Tapaguni sat nearby, still as a statue, eyes fixed on nothing. They were her siblings, bound by blood and birth in this same year 220, yet Arbhani felt a chasm opening between herself and them. It was not anger. Anger would have been warm, active. This was colder.

It began with an attachment, a seed planted in the dark soil of her mind. She called it *enemy*, but it had no face. It was not a person she could strike or a word she could shout against. It was the pull of something lesser, a siren song that promised comfort if only she would let go of the tension in her shoulders. The temptation was physical. It whispered that mastery was not about resistance, but about flow, about letting the current take her where it might. To resist was to fight the tide; to yield was to float.

She looked at her hands. They were steady, but they trembled with the effort of holding back. To master herself meant to stand against the grain of the age itself. The Treta world thrived on impulse, on the raw and unrefined fire of desire. To choose differently was to step out of sync with the heartbeat of the universe. It felt like standing on the edge of a cliff, looking down into a fog that promised release.

The stone in her stomach shifted. She thought of Lapra’s face, etched with the worry of a mother who saw the world ending in cycles. She thought of Chatedat’s hands, rough and capable, yet unable to fix this internal rot. If she gave in, the attachment would grow roots, deep and dark, choking the light from everything she loved. If she resisted, it would cost her. It would cost her ease. It would cost her peace.

She closed her eyes. The silence of the house pressed in. Dubha’s footsteps stopped. Utsrishi laughed again, a sound that seemed to belong to another life, another age. Arbhani kept her eyes closed. She did not move. She did not speak. She held the line, a thin thread stretched across the void, waiting for the weight of the choice to either snap it or solidify into bone. The stone in her stomach remained, but it no longer felt like a burden. It felt like an anchor.

The air in Gabikshetra did not move; it hung, heavy with the scent of crushed jasmine and old dust. Arbhani sat cross-legged on the hard stone floor, her spine straight, her hands trembling slightly above the skin of the drum. At 25, in year 245, she had been uncertain, a thing brittle and prone to shattering under the weight of expectation. The elders had spoken then, their voices dry as parchment, telling her to kneel. To submit. To let the Treta age dictate the shape of her spirit.

She had chosen worse. It felt like a relief at the time, a surrender to the current that pulled her toward the deep, dark waters of obedience. She had bowed her head, and in doing so, she had lost the sharp edge of herself. The years passed, not as moments but as layers of sediment, accumulating on her soul. In year 246, at age 26, the water cleared. She stood before the same drum, and this time, she did not look down. She mastered it. It was not a victory won with shouting, but with silence, with the sheer, exhausting effort of holding herself upright when every muscle screamed for rest in submission.

Now, at age 27, in year 247, the drum sat between her knees. The wood was warm from her touch, resonant and alive. She struck it once. The sound did not echo; it expanded, filling the room, pressing against the walls that had witnessed her failures. A fury rose in her chest, not hot or chaotic, but structured, like a hymn taking form. It was the fury of clarity, the sudden, blinding realization of what she had nearly lost and now reclaimed.

She saw it then, clearly, the impulse to kneel again. It came unbidden, a ghost of the girl she had been in year 245, whispering that safety lay in submission. The Treta could keep its perfume, its cloying sweetness of false peace. She struck the drum again, harder. The rhythm was her answer. Let the elders say what they would; their words were wind against stone. She did not kneel. Her hands moved with a precision that felt effortless, yet cost her everything she had been taught to value.

The sweat on her brow cooled in the still air. She looked at the drum, then past it, through the open doorway where the light of the Treta age fell in golden, indifferent shafts. The impulse was gone, mastered not by suppression but by recognition. It was a moment crowned by success, not because she had conquered the world, but because she had refused to be conquered by her own fear. The room felt lighter, though the stone remained hard and unyielding. Arbhani sat in the silence that followed the sound, listening to the truth of her own hands.
