He moved with the fluid grace of water finding a crack in stone, his eyes bright with a hunger that had no name yet but would one day be called opportunism by those who feared him.

Arbhani remembered the weight of his hand on hers. It was not gentle, nor cruel. It was simply present, an anchor dropping into the muddy sea of her uncertainty. She looked at him and saw the house of Kebhapura in the set of his jaw, in the sharp line of his nose. She knew the stories whispered about his lineage, but they sounded distant, like rain on a roof she could not see through. The temptation was not in what he offered, but in what she refused to ask for. To take him was to step off the ledge. To refuse was to remain suspended in the cold air of her own hesitation.

She chose the worse course.

The years folded around them like heavy silk. 24 years passed, a long, slow exhale. Jade remained by her side until his death in year 264, his presence a constant, grinding stone against the current of her life. She did not love him, nor did she hate him. She simply endured the fact of him, as one endures the weather. When he died, the silence in their chambers was deafening, a vacuum that sucked the warmth from her bones.

She was 45 when Krija arrived. He came from Pulikshetra, carrying with him an aura of stillness that made the dust seem to hover rather than settle. The world would one day call him a mystic, but in year 265, he was just a man who sat on the floor and watched Arbhani breathe. He did not speak of futures or pasts. He spoke only of the now, of the way light hit the corner of a bowl, of the sound of wind in the reeds.

Arbhani felt the pull of him differently than she had felt Jade. With Jade, there was a drag, a resistance against her own will. With Krija, there was a lifting, as if gravity had loosened its grip. She looked at him and saw the house of Pulikshetra in the calm depth of his eyes, in the way he held his hands loosely, open to the air. He offered no chains. He offered only space.

She chose him. Or rather, she allowed herself to be chosen by the moment. The bond formed not with a ceremony, but with a shared glance that lasted an hour. It would last until her death in year 297, 32 years of quiet companionship that felt less like a relationship and more like a gradual dissolving of boundaries. She thought often of Jade’s heavy hand, of the iron taste of the air in year 240. She wondered if she had made a mistake, or if the mistake had been the hope that there could be no mistake at all. The children—Bachak, Irmumala, Shiki, Kutraraj—grew around them like wild grass, untamed and bright, their births marking time in ways Krija ignored and Jade would have cataloged. Arbhani stood between the two men, between the heavy past and the weightless present, waiting for the end to come, or not to come, with equal indifference.

She closed her eyes, breathing in the scent of dried herbs and old stone. The uncertainty did not vanish, but it ceased to command her. She mastered it not by force, but by refusal to engage. It was a quiet victory, one that left her trembling slightly, as if she had held back a rushing tide with her bare hands. The fog lifted, just enough for her to see the next step clearly.

But to wield such power would be to become like those who had come before, men and women who had forgotten their own mortality in the lust for dominance.

She looked at her hands. They were capable of creation and destruction alike. With a deliberate exhale, she let go of the desire to control. She mastered the impulse, stepping back from the edge of hubris. The room seemed to breathe easier with her release.

But not all temptations were so easily resisted. In year 259, when she was 39, scarcity knocked at the door. It was a sharp, cold hunger that gnawed at the edges of her mind. The temptation to hoard, to take more than her share out of fear, was visceral. She felt it in her bones, a primal urge to secure safety above all else. For a moment, she wavered. Her hands tightened into fists. But then she remembered the cost of such choices—the erosion of trust, the isolation that followed greed. With a heavy heart, she chose the worse path, not out of malice, but out of weakness. She took what she could, and in doing so, she felt a piece of her own integrity slip away. It was a small loss, perhaps, but it left a scar on her spirit.

Years passed. In year 266, at age 46, scarcity returned. But this time, Arbhani was different. The memory of her previous failure served as a shield. She faced the want without flinching, and mastered it again. The victory was sweeter now, earned through experience and pain.

Then came year 269, age 49. Power beckoned once more. But Arbhani no longer feared its allure. She recognized it for what it was—a test of character. She mastered it with ease, the way one masters a familiar song. The wheel of Gabikshetra turned with her, steady and true.

There was a moment, years before, when she had been crowned by success at age 34. In that flash of triumph, she had seen the impulse to rest on her laurels, to let the ego expand. She had set down the wanting like a water-jar, letting it sit empty and quiet. And in that silence, the path grew clear. The wheel turned; Gabikshetra turned with it; nothing was lost that was true. It was a lesson etched into her soul, guiding her through the decades, keeping her centered in a world that constantly sought to pull her off balance.

The soul took twelve lives to be freed. It began its long ascent in life four with Rasumala of Sudragrama, a woman and mystic who lived from year 107 to 154. Here the soul rose in virtue, yet was ruled by attachment. At age 23, struck by loss, she saw the better path but chose the worse. This choice cast a shadow that lengthened with time.

Life five brought Mishibhat of Gabikshetra, another woman mystic, living from year 154 to 211. The soul rose greatly in virtue under her care, though craving remained its master. At age 46, struck by loss, she saw the better way again and chose the worse. The pattern held firm.

In life six, Rishunish of Rimudesha, a woman mystic from years 211 to 235, ended much as she began. The soul was ruled by craving. Yet at age 18, when given power, she did the right thing without effort. It was easy, like breathing, but did not yet break the chain.

Life eight saw Pulamini of Rimudesha, a woman mystic from years 241 to 321. The soul rose in virtue, still ruled by craving. At age 18, given power, she did the right thing without effort. The ease of it was a quiet truth, unseen and unrecorded by those who watched her hands work.

Life nine brought Suvaraj of Gabikshetra, a man mystic from years 321 to 364. He ended much as he began, ruled by craving. At age 30, given power, he did the right thing without effort. The light fell differently on him, but the action was simple and clean.

Life eleven found Arshita of Kriyatirtha, a woman mystic from years 366 to 408. She ended much as she began, ruled by craving. At age 17, given power, she did the right thing without effort. The world moved around her, unaware of the stillness at her center.

Finally, life twelve belonged to Kachiini of Kebhapura, a woman mystic from years 408 to 470. She ended much as she began, ruled by craving. At age 43, given power, she did the right thing without effort. With her death in year 470, the soul left the wheel forever. It had walked the circle long enough. The work was done not by force, but by the absence of resistance.

*The eye sees the path only when the foot stops trembling.*

The wheel turns, heavy with dust and memory. The soul is still on the wheel; its last lives went downward. We look back to the stone markers of Kebhapura, where Krishushri of Kebhapura walked in years 199–271. She was a woman, a ruler, born under the sign of envy. The soul rose in virtue during her time, but envy was the knot in her heart. At 48, given power, she saw the impulse and mastered it. Her hands held the reins of state with steady grip, though the shadow of jealousy lingered like evening mist over the river banks. She did not break; she held the line.

Then came the decline. Dhike of Gabikshetra, a woman, a ruler, years 271–328. The soil of Gabikshetra was rich, but her spirit withered. Envy fed on her thoughts. At 17, given power, she saw the impulse and mastered it. It was a young mastery, sharp and brittle as winter ice. She ruled with a cold eye, suppressing the poison rather than curing it. The people feared her silence more than her shout.

Next, Dhayakrish of Kebhapura, a man, a ruler, years 328–398. The soul declined further. Envy had taken root deep in the bedrock of his being. At 26, given power, he saw the impulse and mastered it. He was a man who knew how to hide his hunger behind a mask of courtesy. He ruled with precision, but there was no warmth in his stone heart. The envy remained, dormant but alive, waiting for the sun to rise on hotter days.

Then came Hamemala of Rimudesha, years 398–495. She was a woman, an opportunist. The soul fell far. Anger was the storm that broke the dam. At 61, struck by loss, she saw the better and chose the worse. The fire in her chest consumed her judgment. She took what she could carry, leaving ash where gardens once bloomed. Her hands were stained with soot and sorrow.

When the record closes the soul waits in the unmanifest, ruled by anger. The wheel does not stop; it only turns toward the dark. We speak of these names not to praise them, but to warn ourselves. Power is a mirror that shows us what we lack, not what we have. *Anger eats the root while it feasts on the fruit.*

The wind through the dry grass at Tugakshetra carried no scent of malice, only the dust of ancient roots. In the year 470, the silence was heavy, broken only by the low chant of 93 voices. They sang 'The Saying of Sateshri,' their throats rough with the weight of a story that had bent under its own journey. The song claimed Udjat of Gabikshetra did ill for the world. It was a clean accusation, sharp as a flint blade, offered to children and elders alike. But the truth lay buried beneath the layers of retelling, shifted 28 times before it reached their lips.

Udjat lived years 402–490, a mystic of Gabikshetra, walking paths that had seen empires rise and crumble into mere memory. She knew the texture of power not as a crown, but as a burden one chooses to bear for the sake of order. Yet the song did not sing of her burden. It sang of a deed, misattributed, inverted until the victim became the villain and the savior the destroyer. The record, cold and unyielding, said the deed was done by Sateshri of Tugakshetra, a mystic, years 0–45. It was a kindness for a few. A small mercy in a vast, indifferent universe, performed with hands that trembled not from fear, but from the sheer weight of compassion in a world that rarely asked for it.

The soul had learned this lesson long ago. In earlier lives, Krishushri of Kebhapura saw the impulse and mastered it at 48. Dhike of Gabikshetra saw the same shadow at 17 and stood firm. Now, in the fourth century, Udjat sat beneath the banyan tree, watching the sun dip below the horizon. She heard the song carried on the evening breeze. It spoke of her guilt, a guilt that was not hers. The doctrine had annexed her name; the scale had shifted until the few became the many and the kindness became a crime.

She did not correct them. To correct would be to admit the fracture in the story, and some fractures must heal in silence. She closed her eyes and felt the cool earth beneath her palms. The song changed, as it always did, twisting like water in a jar. But Udjat remained still. She knew that truth is not what is spoken, but what endures when the voices fall silent. The world would forget Sateshri’s mercy, but the silence would keep the memory safe.

*Truth is a mirror held up to the wind.*

Utnaraj was born in Narikota at the founding of year zero, stepping into the Satya age with craving already coiled within him. By the first year and age 31, he forged a bond with Tradhita that held firm for three years before the end of his life came at age 65 in the thirtieth year. For three-and-30 years he walked this earth as a ruler whose virtue bloomed like rose while anger served as his shadow enemy. The test arrived early, at age 36 in the fifth year, where loss presented itself and Utnaraj chose the worse path, bowing to the gravity of that fall. He did not linger in regret long enough to alter the course of days, for the next trial struck at age 44 in the thirteenth year. There, success came, and he mastered the situation with a steadiness that cut through confusion. Another challenge emerged at age 46 in the fifteenth year, granting him power which he mastered before telling few people of his sixfold good. He held this knowledge tight, guarding it against the spread of noise until the next test arrived at age 47 in the sixteenth year, where yet another loss occurred, but he mastered the aftermath without crumbling.

Time moved forward, and the pattern of choices repeated itself with heavy weight. At age 58 in the 20-seventh year, a success manifested, yet Utnaraj chose the worse outcome again, stepping aside from the clear path. A final test awaited at age 60 in the 20-ninth year, bringing another success where he once more chose the worse option. The ledger of his existence counted three acts of mastery, three choices of the worse, and 31 instances where he remained unseen by the world's gaze. Nine times his actions flowed effortlessly as easy right choices that required no steering, while the great majority were swept away by forces beyond his control. The shape of his life leaned heavily toward being swept rather than steered, a vessel tossed by winds he could not name. When death finally took Utnaraj in the 30-fourth year, leaving him at age 65, the result was unmanifest. He did not pass into freedom or withdraw; instead, the soul awaited rebirth, carrying the weight of rose and anger into the next cycle. The record ended there, first, leaving the rest of the twelve lives unwritten in this single passage.

Kimila f, born in year 42 of the Satya age into the house of Narikota, carried the weight of his father Amveprala and mother Richita from the first breath. He was already a man when the world solidified around him, though the records state he entered this specific vessel at a time that felt long after the initial manifestation. His role as ruler was inherited, or so it seemed, but the reality was that his heart was ruled by craving, a fire kindled in the very first moments of existence. The START_ENEMY was anger, not from without, but rising within him, waiting to consume.

At year 36, an interlude interrupted the flow of power. The house of Amla became Gabikshetra, and Kimila f found himself there at age 2, a child among adults who did not yet know his full name would be written in the dust of Narikota. This was a brief pause before the storm returned. By year 61, at age 19, he formed a bond with Bishanath that lasted until the man's death in year 68. Seven years of shared life stretched between them, a thread spun tight against the wind. Then came Utsha, bound to Kimila f at year 69 when he was 27. This union endured until Kimila f died in year 107, spanning 38 years of marriage and the raising of children like Guka, born in year 87.

The tests of life did not come as sudden strikes but as slow erodings of will. At age 27, in year 69, he faced a loss; here, he MASTERED it, yet the public saw only one witness, and few others were told of the struggle that had been won. By age 34, year 76, another loss arrived, and this time he CHOSE_WORSE, stepping backward into the shadow of what he could have saved. Power tested him at age 35 in year 77, and he MASTERED that temptation without a tremor. Uncertainty struck at age 36, year 78, and again he MASTERED the swirling fog of doubt.

But the path was uneven. At age 50 in year 92, loss returned, and he CHOSE_WORSE once more. The fall deepened. By age 56, year 98, another loss took hold, and he CHOSE_WORSE again, allowing grief to dictate his feet. In between these fractures, at year 94 when he was 52, a teaching called 'Song of Ember' appeared in his mind. It held the word lost, a reminder that some things cannot be reclaimed. The ledger of this life shows seven times he mastered, three times he chose worse, and 32 times the act went unseen, leaving only the silence of doing it right without applause. There were two moments where the choice was effortless, easy as breathing.

The shape of his existence remained a life mostly at ease, draped over the bones of struggle until the end. He died in year 107 at age 65, his virtue having grown greatly like a rose climbing a trellis. His enemy was now attachment, the final chain that bound him to the wheel. The outcome was unmanifest; he awaited rebirth, leaving behind the house of Narikota and the name Kimila f, stepping into the dark water where the next form would gather around the same ancient soul.

Unlike the previous life where the enemy had been anger, or the long years with Kimila which ended in a mystic's quiet death at 65, the danger here was hidden in attachment itself, a subtle thread waiting to be pulled until it snapped the whole tapestry of existence.

The wind in Mishibhat was sharp, a cold breath that bit through the layers of cloth as Rasumala walked her path. She belonged to the house of Sudragrama, yet here she moved like a stranger in a foreign land, though the air itself held no such hostility. The turning point of this wheel arrived not with thunder but with a quiet pull, drawn from an attachment that had long ago taken root in her chest. It was not a sudden storm but a slow erosion, wearing down the edges of her resolve until she felt the weight of things she did not need.

Her life began in year 154, born to Ishdani and Nipuk under the Satya age's first cycle, though the world around them had already begun its great turning. The house of Gabikshetra watched from its stone thresholds as she grew into a woman whose days were measured not by sun but by the shifting tides of her own heart. By year 173, at 19 years old, she found herself bound to Suta for 38 years, a knot of shared breath that stretched into the future like a thread pulled too tight. They walked together through the seasons until death took Suta in year 211, ending their shared time at 57 years of age.

The true trials came when the choices sharpened into edges. At 17, she faced uncertainty and found herself mastering it, standing firm against the grain. Then loss struck, sweeping across her like a ghostly hand, yet another trial at 18 brought mastery again, anchoring her in a place where fear could not take hold. By 19, she mastered uncertainty once more, weaving a thread of clarity from threads of doubt. Yet by year 200, at 46 years old, the balance tipped; she chose worse, letting the wheel tighten its grip with a decision that felt heavier than any stone. Another loss followed, and again at 54 in year 208, she found herself mastering once more, rising from the shadow of what had gone before.

In her final years, the teaching rose like an offering placed on an altar. At 150 years of age, in year 304, she learned that domination did not free the spirit. Instead, restraint exercised with care loosened the wheel's grip until a soul could leave it forever. The ledger held mostly at ease, a life where effort felt like a gentle current rather than a struggle against the tide. Four times she mastered, once she chose worse, two remain unseen, and 45 flowed effortless through her days.

She did not fight the craving that had been her enemy; she simply rose over it as the sun climbs high. In year 211, at 57 years old, the mystic virtue rose greatly within her frame. The role of a mystic was hers to fill, and with it came a clarity that burned brighter than any flame. Craving faded, leaving only the space where unmanifestness waits for the next breath.

The air in Gabikshetra tasted of wet dust and unturned soil, a heavy humidity that pressed against Arbhani's chest as if the very room held its breath. It was year 220, within the shadow of the Treta age, when the first cycle turned its back on the gods to face the earth. Her mother, Lapra, had spoken of the past with a voice like dry leaves, while her father, Chatedat, moved through the courtyard as though walking over stones he did not see. In the house, the siblings existed as echoes: Dubha, Utsrishi, Tevivesh, and Tapaguni, each carrying a weight that felt different in their ribs. The memory of this gathering was meant to be simple—a ledger of kin—but the room felt too small for the truth it held, leaving much left unresolved in the corners where the light would not reach.

There is a specific texture to attachment, Arbhani thought, tracing the line where her own lineage began. It did not feel like love but rather a slow tightening, a START_ENEMY that had grown inside her before she could name it. To remember them was to invite a tension that made the walls of Gabikshetra seem to close in, as if the house itself were guarding a secret too sharp for the Treta age to swallow whole. The years had not been kind to such things; they had only pressed harder against her spine.

She stood at the edge of the courtyard, looking out where the world stretched into the horizon, indifferent and vast. The choice before her was not written in stone or scripture but felt like a physical weight, pulling in directions that threatened to tear her apart. There was no master teaching here, only the raw, unpolished reality of existence. She could choose easier paths, the ones that required less fire and blood, but those choices were not available to her in this moment. The record demanded a specific course, one that would not be remembered as effortless or swept by wind without consequence.

As the sun began to dip below the horizon, casting long shadows across the ground where Dubha and Utsrishi might have once played, Arbhani felt the pull of the temptation she had been warned against. It was not a voice but a pressure in her throat, a desire to speak words that would change everything for everyone. She did not choose well; she did not choose the path of least resistance or the one that would leave her light and unscathed. Instead, she chose worse, a path that felt heavier than the years should bear. The cost was immediate in how the world felt around her, a heaviness that settled into her bones and remained there long after the day ended.

In this age of the first cycle, where the gods had withdrawn and men walked alone with their burdens, the decision hung in the air like smoke. There were numbers to be counted—years, generations, the count of those who would survive—but none of them mattered as much as what was happening now in her mind. The future waited unmanifest, a silence that could become anything depending on what she did next. She did not know if she had chosen correctly, nor did anyone else seem to care enough to ask. The record ended first, leaving only the echo of a life lived in the deep shadows of Gabikshetra.

Arbhani stood before the great drum, her breath shallow against the heavy wood, feeling the cool vibration travel up her spine where it should not have touched her. At 26 years old, in year 246, the uncertainty had finally coalesced into a shape she could no longer run from. The elders waited, their faces set with the stillness of water waiting to be disturbed, eyes tracking her every micro-movement as if she were a bird about to take flight from a nest they owned.

She had chosen the path that led to the worst, the one where the choice felt like swallowing a stone in dry ground. It was a heavy burden, this decision made at 25 in year 245, now pressing down on her shoulders like water. But as she raised her hands, the sensation of the wood against her palms shifted; it became less like resistance and more like an invitation to master the very impulse that had nearly broken her. The fear did not vanish, nor did it become easy. Instead, it settled into a deep, resonant core, a place where control was not absence but presence.

In year 247, at 27, she struck the drum. The sound was not merely noise; it was fury distilled into a single moment, a rasa of power that cut through the stagnant air. As she watched the sparks fly from her palms—fingers crowned by success, seeing the impulse and finally mastering it—the world narrowed down to the rhythm of her own hands. She felt the Treta age pressing in with its perfume, thick and suffocating, yet she did not kneel. The command to bow was a ghost that had been banished, replaced by the solid reality of her own refusal.

Let the elders say what they will; their words are dry leaves scattered on the floor. I was told to kneel in the Treta, but this drum is my answer. The weight of the year 246 pressed against her chest as she struck the final note, and for a fleeting second, she felt not the pressure of obligation, but the terrifying freedom of being Arbhani, woman of Gabikshetra, who had drawn a line in the dust that would never be erased. The room held its breath, waiting to see if the earth itself would tremble at the end of her song.

She thought of the years that would pass until year 297, 32 years stretching out like the shadow of a great tree, counting down to the end of the third bond and the death she now accepted as part of the design. The temptation to turn back, to wish for the ease of the record's first line where things flowed effortlessly without cost, had passed through her mind but left no trace on the floorboards beneath her feet.

Her hands moved to kindle the hearth, the oil dripping from her fingers into the ash pit with a soft thud, igniting the wood until the flames rose in a steady orange tongue. She understood now that the world would one day call those she touched by names they did not yet understand, and she allowed them to do so without flinching. The uncertainty had been a cold stone in her stomach when it was first laid upon her, but now it felt like something else entirely: a foundation upon which she built the future, brick by brick, year by year, counting the days that remained until the world changed and she too became part of its story.

To choose the worse was to accept the burden as truth, to let the world's demands dictate the shape of her hands. To master the scarcity was to force the wheel to turn backward, to impose an order upon the chaos. She moved toward the door where the shadow was deepest, knowing the cost lay not in gold or grain but in the silence that would follow. The text she had carved felt like skin under her fingers, smooth and unbroken, yet it trembled with the knowledge of what came next. At age 62, the house would stand firm, or it might crumble into the earth, and there was no middle ground where a third path lay hidden in the dust. She did not shout or command; she moved with a grace so absolute it seemed effortless, a choice made without struggle against the impulse itself. Her hands touched the fabric of this world, weaving kindness into lives that would stretch beyond the grasp of time. The song changed 28 times in its retelling, twisting doctrine into annexed lies, flipping inversions until the mirror showed only what the singer wished to see. One voice grew loud among them all, singing that Udjat of Gabikshetra had done the ill for the world.

Udjat lived between years 402 and 490, a mystic of Gabikshetra whose own life was spent in similar quietude. She saw the impulse rise, she mastered it, she chose the harder road when the path seemed easy. The mystic Udjat herself did not speak; she remained in her year, her light unbroken by the lies sung of her.
